articles.text: Editor: We seek your assistance in making sure that Piedmont Firefighters are accorded salaries and health benefits in keeping with the fact that they are our Piedmont citizens’ extended family in terms of their dedication to our health and safety. We moved to Piedmont in 1993 and raised our two children here. We have experienced the intelligence, caring and decision-making of our Piedmont Firefighters. Had we not personally benefited from the firefighters’ kindness and skill, we would still feel tremendous gratitude to them for being here just in case. We were very distressed to read the article in the September 23 Piedmont Post indicating that negotiations between the firefighters and the city are at a standstill. We carefully read the firefighters’ concerns about the necessity of 1) having pay increases to encourage longevity, and 2) having retirement benefits to cover firefighters’ medical care for the period between retirement and Social Security eligibility. We share the firefighters’ underlying concern about inadequate staffing which requires excessive overtime to keep us safe. As residents and taxpayers, we support the firefighters’ demands. Piedmont prides itself on being a city that is at the forefront of good decision-making. Piedmont needs to step up to support the firefighters and to inform its citizens what efforts and finances are required to do so. We rely on Piedmont Firefighters for our lives and the lives of our children. Is there anything more important? The firefighters’ knowledge, skills, courage and work ethic should be celebrated and honored by accepting their demands. We are both retired attorneys; Joe represented injured workers and clients denied social security disability; I practiced civil rights law. As residents of Piedmont, we find the city’s response puzzling and extraordinarily short-sighted (using overtime instead of properly hiring, making the very hiring process discouraging by not providing the enticement of raises after certain years of service are reached, by not meeting the basic human need of health insurance until Social Security eligibility is reached). We look forward to hearing from you. –Susan Goldsmith and Joseph Waxman
articles.title: City needs to fix hiring procedure at Fire Dept.

articles.text: Editor, We are writing to Piedmont voters to urge a YES vote on Measure GG. Our families planted roots in Piedmont more than 100 years ago. We have made our home here because Piedmont offers a unique combination of small-town ambiance with strong public safety, outstanding public schools and excellent quality of life amenities such as beautiful parks, strong recreation programs and lovely public spaces. We believe the financial experts who are telling us we soon will have a shortfall in revenues to pay for existing city services, facilities and infrastructure. The cuts that will come if that happens, most likely starting with “quality of life” expenses, threaten the things we hold most dear about Piedmont. We believe the small increase in the real estate transfer tax proposed by Measure GG is the most painless method of dealing with the threat. It is only imposed at a time when property is being sold—a time when funds are most likely to be available to make a payment. Your YES vote on Measure GG will help preserve the Piedmont that has kept our families here for so long. –Fran Bishopric Wolfe and Cameron Wolfe, Jr.
articles.title: Yes on Measure GG

articles.text: Editor, Having served eight years on the Piedmont City Council, including two years as mayor, I understand deeply that the true measure of public service is not the popularity of every individual decision; it is whether the institution is stronger, more accountable, and better prepared for the future when one’s service concludes. That is why I am again supporting Dr. Cindi Reiss for the Peralta Community College District Board. When I endorsed Cindi in 2022, I noted her educational and accreditation experience, devotion to the common good, attention to detail, intellect and vision. I also recognized her willingness to challenge entrenched interests in pursuit of sound fiscal management. When she ran for the Board in 2018, Peralta faced serious financial instability, accreditation concerns, leadership turnover, board conflict, board micromanagement of chancellors and possible state-takeover of the district. Cindi Reiss has fulfilled those promises. Today, Peralta is financially and institutionally stronger. Its four colleges are fully accredited. Stable executive leadership, stronger financial practices, greater transparency, and more disciplined longrange planning have replaced years of instability. Recent credit ratings reflect increased confidence in the District’s governance and financial direction, while a 2025 bond-refunding transaction saved taxpayers $13.7 million. These gains did not happen by accident. Cindi helped foster a Board culture focused on its proper responsibilities: setting policy, safeguarding public resources, requiring accountability, and supporting strong professional leadership without micromanaging it. She has also demonstrated the courage to make difficult decisions when the district’s long-term interests required them. But recovery is not completion. Peralta must now carry its Transformation Plan from vision into implementation. That means reducing fragmentation, coordinating programs and services, strengthening pathways for students, and building a fiscal structure capable of sustaining the colleges well beyond the tenure of any trustee or administrator. As Piedmont residents, we have a direct stake in Peralta’s future, in its strength and success. Whether it’s through our many Piedmont high school students that have participated in dual enrollment with Peralta by taking Calculus III: Partial Differentiation, Discrete Mathematics, Linear Algebra or business management classes; adults that have taken art and language classes, or through the thousands of students that Peralta’s colleges serve in Alameda County, Piedmont benefits from a strong Peralta Community College system. When Peralta helps students earn degrees, certificates or transfer to universities, and build economically secure lives, the benefits extend well beyond its campuses. A strong Peralta means a stronger regional workforce, greater economic mobility, responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars, and a healthier and more stable East Bay. Our support of Peralta’s colleges is an investment in the regional institutions and quality of life on which Piedmont itself depends. I urge my fellow Piedmonters to reelect Dr. Cindi Reiss as Peralta Community College District Trustee, Area 5, on November 3. Best, Teddy Gray King
articles.title: Reelect Dr. Cindi Reiss as Peralta Community College District Trustee, Area 5

articles.text: Dear Editor, When I was young, Piedmont Recreation Department programs were instrumental in my development and helped form the person I am today. When I was fortunate enough to serve as Piedmont’s Recreation Director and later as City Administrator, I gained insight into the ongoing cost of the many services provided by the City of Piedmont to the community. From streets to parks, sidewalks to police cars, fire apparatus to building maintenance, the costs to provide essential services to Piedmont have continued to rise. Piedmont is one of a small number of California cities whose revenues are primarily property based. This funding structure severely limits options for increased revenues needed to keep Piedmont from falling further behind. Measure GG is a reasonable way to provide additional and ongoing funds to support city services, while not placing an ongoing burden on property owners. If approved, Measure GG will bring Piedmont’s transfer tax more in line with our surrounding communities and provide approximately $1.5 million in additional revenue to support essential services and city infrastructure. Piedmonters understand the value of ongoing investment, especially in community services and assets. Supporting Measure GG is a way to keep up and keep Piedmont moving forward for years to come. Sincerely, Sara Lillevand Retired City Administrator threats. Council. Sincerely,

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department is asking community members to complete a brief disaster preparedness survey by October 30. The survey will measure changes since 2024 and help guide future preparedness efforts. Preparedness knowledge and actions have changed since the city’s first community survey in 2024. This survey will help the city understand how prepared the community is for earthquakes, wildfires, and other disasters. The survey should take about 5-7 minutes to complete and is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ DisasterSurvey. The city’s 2024 survey showed that many respondents recognized disaster risk but had not taken some basic preparedness steps. Among respondents: • 73% were registered for AC Alert • 22% had a current household emergency communication plan • 34% had a current two-week emergency water supply • 27% felt confident or very confident in their knowledge of how to prepare for disasters This year’s survey revisits many of these measures and includes new questions about how the city’s preparedness efforts have developed. This includes earthquake safety and steps that residents can take to minimize wildfire risks at home. The survey will ask where people turn for information during an emergency, what gets in the way of becoming better prepared, and what kinds of resources would be most useful. Since the 2024 survey, Piedmont Fire has expanded preparedness outreach and community engagement, including: • Updating Piedmont’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan with extensive community participation • Increasing education about wildfire home hardening and defensible space, including a series of presentations to community groups • Conducting a practical wildfire evacuation exercise in the Blair/Scenic/Alta neighborhood and creating an at-home evacuation exercise available to all households • Continuing year-round outreach on emergency alerts, evacuation readiness, and household preparedness The survey data will help the city evaluate where the work is having an impact and what gaps remain. It will also establish a stronger baseline for earthquake preparedness as Piedmont Fire looks to expand outreach in this area. Results will help guide future communications, educational resources, exercises, and community programs. Complete the survey by October 30 at piedmont.ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. articles.text: At the September 22 City Council meeting, the Council voted to award the Moraga Avenue Pedestrian Safety Project contract to Terocons Inc. for $785,533. The project will install safety improvements as recommended in the Piedmont Safer Streets Plan. Construction is expected to begin in early October along Moraga Avenue between Ramona Avenue and Red Rock Avenue. The project will install bulbouts and high-visibility crosswalk striping at the intersection of Ramona and Moraga. The intersection of Monticello & Moraga will receive a landscaped pedestrian refuge island and high-visibility crosswalk striping. The last intersection, Mesa & Moraga, will receive a bulb-out, flashing beacons, and a repositioned crosswalk for improved visibility. Interim Public Works Director Rich Cunningham presented the project to the City Council, detailing some of the changes the project will make. “The intersection between Moraga and Monticello, which you have to walk 120 feet across that intersection to cross it, was not safe, and so we’ve put a traffic island there. Part of that traffic island is set aside for landscape, and we’re bringing water across the street from the cemetery planted area via a pipe that will be installed before paving the Moraga Avenue section. The design also includes preservation of the bike lane,” said Cunningham. The city will fund the project through an Alameda County Transportation Commission (ACTC) grant, which awarded the city $748,000 for design and construction. The ACTC funds transportation improvements throughout Alameda County that facilitate safe, efficient, and accessible travel for all types of transportation. The City’s 2021 Safer Streets Plan identified the Mesa/Moraga intersection as the highest-priority location for citywide pedestrian safety enhancements, prioritizing intersections based on proximity to a school, location on an arterial street, and inclusion on a bike/bus route. Moraga Avenue is one of the few arterial roadways within the City of Piedmont eligible for regional transportation funding. “There’s been almost uniform support across the community. We got a lot of nice emails, proactive people up and down Moraga who are all for it,” said Cunningham. The contract agreement with Terocons Inc. is for 16 weeks to complete the work.

articles.text: On Monday, October 5, Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee announced that Children’s Fairyland has secured a $5,000,000 allocation from the state of California to close out phase one of its capital investment in the park. The funds are designed to facilitate the initial stages of restoration and revitalization. “It’s really a storybook that comes to life. Regardless of how old you are or young you are, my family can attest to the fact, this is a dream come true,” said Lee. Children’s Fairyland CEO Kymberly Miller elucidated the details of the funding, $3,000,000 will be designated to the park’s capital investment to make “sure we are taking care of this physical space for 76 more years.” The remaining two million will go to the park’s general operations. The funds come from the state’s budget which has allocated $14 million for Oakland community organizations, small businesses, public safety, and transitional housing. Other Oakland institutions receiving state funding include: Juntos Fruitvale Cultural Arts Center, Samuel Merritt University’s human trafficking prevention initiative, commercial corridors across Oakland, the city’s Department of Violence Prevention and The Holland transitional housing facility. “For 76 years, Fairyland has given Oakland’s children a place to imagine what’s possible. I still remember bringing my sons here, and today we’re making sure the next generation gets that same magic. This $5 million is a proud victory for Oakland because every dollar we put into community spaces comes back to us in the children they raise,” said Lee. Children’s Fairyland has been a vital part of Oakland’s culture since opening in 1950. As the park that pioneered children’s entertainment in this country, Fairyland forever changed the landscape of “family fun” as it is known today. Children’s Fairyland is ten acres of green space on the shores of Lake Merritt, designed for outdoor play and low-tech, high-touch hands-on learning. It is a rare and increasingly precious resource for children. The $5 million allocation will fund numerous initiatives within Fairyland’s strategic capital investment plan, including essential infrastructure and facility upgrades. Miller describes the funding as foundational, rather than final. “This funding is a launchpad, not a landing place. We have much more work to do to create the Fairyland of tomorrow. We’re deeply grateful to Governor Newsom, Mayor Lee, and our State of California partners for recognizing what Fairyland means to this community, to Oakland, and to the entire Bay Area. We are laying the groundwork for Fairyland’s financial sustainability so we can continue to be a safe and inclusive environment for playOakland Mayor Barbara Lee (left) and Fairyland CEO Kymberly Miller announced the state has granted Children’s Fairyland $5,000,000 from the 2026-27 state budget. ing and learning, where children build critical literacy skills and grow both socially and emotionally,” said Miller. The state funding is a commitment to ensure the 76-year-old iconic and beloved Oakland destination remains a safe, vibrant, and accessible oasis for generations to come. It also signals a broader shift underway at Fairyland. As an organization upheld and supported by its community, admissions, memberships, and the generosity of donors of all kinds, Children’s Fairyland is now adding the kind of institutional support it needs to fuel the next phase of its modernization. Learn more at Fairyland.org.

The assembly, organized by acting teacher Kim Taylor, junior Stella Joseph, and senior Ben Ramakrishnan, involved current PHS students reading real stories from anonymous PHS graduates about their experiences involving sexual assault and consent. “The purpose of the Consent Assembly is to bring awareness and educate people about how to stay safe and how to prevent these stories from happening again,” junior Ida Marshall said. Marshall was one of 16 students who read stories. Although Marshall is enrolled in acting, students do not need to take acting to present in the assembly. A goal of the assembly is for people from across the school to be involved. “I think it went well. All of the other story readers were really talented and I thought we made the stories sound really real. I heard stories about people being affected by it,” Marshall said. PHS also has a lunch club, Piedmont for Consent (P4C), that focuses on spreading awareness about consent. According to P4C co-president junior Sophia Puckett, the club’s goal is to make sure everyone feels comfortable about consent and their personal boundaries. Puckett said that club events this year include giving presentations about what consent is at elementary schools in Piedmont, along with partnering with an elective class at Piedmont Middle School. “The middle school has a new class that’s going to help us lead presentations for the elementary school. It’s called LEAD,” Puckett said. “It’s an elective class, and it focuses on consent next semester.” P4C co-president junior Lucy Shoop said that they are working on a middle school assembly as well. “We’re working on a script that the middle schoolers are going to use in the new elective. Basically, we’re going to help them teach,” Shoop said. The Consent Assembly happened to coincide with the reopening of a 2024 sexual assault case at Cornell University, which sparked conversations across the PHS campus. Puckett said that Piedmont for Consent held an open conversation at lunch for students to share their thoughts about the case. “I think with the Cornell case, a lot of the stories and conversations can be triggering for a lot of people, and we want to make sure people have a place they can come if they need something,” Puckett said. Although Piedmont for Consent is not directly affiliated with the Consent Assembly, Puckett said that their goals very much align. “The assembly is a great way that we are getting the message of consent culture out to Piedmont and other Bay Area schools,” said Puckett. The Consent Assembly takes place once a year, and Marshall said she hopes to continue her involvement. “I really enjoyed doing it. I thought it was a really meaningful and valuable experience, and I hope I’m able to do it next year,” Marshall said. “I think bringing awareness to this stuff is not talked about enough and that’s why it’s really important.” Julia Stokes is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student writer intern for the Piedmont Post.

They’re hard to miss once you know what you’re looking for: often in wait for prey at the center of giant, wheel-shaped webs— where their family name “orbweaver” comes from—these spiders’ large abdomens range in color from pale cream to bright orange, and their long legs are striped with light and dark colors. But I’ve always loved them, and over the years my kids and I have made a tradition of getting closer rather than backing away. We find a few orbweavers each fall in the park and think of them as our “pets” for the season, returning regularly to watch them spin webs, grow, and change. these adult orbweavers at their biggest and most spectacular, they’re nearing the end of their lives. They’ve reproduced and left behind egg sacs containing the beginnings of another generation. And eventually, the spiders we’ve been watching disappear. articles.text: After years of colleges moving away from requiring standardized testing, the admissions process is shifting once again. As more universities reinstate SAT or ACT requirements, high school students are reconsidering the role tests, like the PSAT, play in their college preparation. During COVID-19, many universities stopped requiring test scores as part of their application process, shifting to test-optional or test-blind. As testing gains popularity, many students view the PSAT as their first step of the college application process. “I took the PSAT to get a baseline of what my score was without studying, so that I could compare it to my preACT score to see which one I was better at,” junior Chiara Silvio said. Students often take these exams in their sophomore year of high school, so they can know which test they want to take and are most confident in junior year. “I wanted to see which one I was better at so junior year I can really focus on studying,” sophomore Naomi Jerez said. Although the PSAT has become increasingly popular, some students are choosing to use other resources to determine which direction they want to go in. “I did not take the PSAT; I didn’t sign up for it because I plan to take the online ones at home,” junior Kyla Williams said. “I was also going to take the SAT in December, January, and another one in March.” As top schools switch to being test-required, it affects students differently depending on their educational experiences and future goals. “A lot of people study for it, and it’s not actually accurate, it’s more about the tools you have available to you than how well you’d naturally do,” Silvio said. While preparation plays a large role in a student’s success when taking a standardized test, each student nationwide is taking the same test. This uniformity provides colleges with a baseline to help determine a student’s admission. “Giving your grades or just your transcript only shows in comparison to your school,” Williams said. “For the SAT, it’s an overall evaluation that doesn’t solely compare to your surroundings.” With the increase in resources available to students, standardized tests help colleges determine how a student truly performs. “Nowadays you can get good grades by taking online classes, and get into a good school,” Jerez said. “With a standardized test, everyone’s taking the same thing, so it’s easier to compare scores objectively.” Taking the PSAT and preACT is not a required step for the real SAT or ACT, and can take multiple hours depending on testing location. PreACT exams were conducted in the PHS STEAM building on Saturday, October 3, starting at 8:45 a.m. and lasting for two hours and 45 minutes. “The test was really draining, and it was a lot harder than I thought it was going to be,” Silvio said. However, many students say the benefits outweigh the effort required. “I’ll be able to know which format I like better and I’ll also get an idea of the test taking environment,” Jerez said. Along with prepping students for the SAT, taking the PSAT offers students a series of other benefits to support their college applications. “You can sign up for National Merit, because it helps you qualify if you take the PSAT,” Williams said. For the class of 2026, many universities have announced their switch from test optional to test required. Cornell University, Yale University, Columbia University and Princeton University are some of many that have announced their change. Many schools have also announced changes to their requirements that won’t take effect for a few more years. The University of California schools (UC Berkeley, UCSB, UCLA, etc.) are still test-free for the fall 2027 admission, and are reviewing whether or not to bring back testing for future applicants, according to the University of California. Ayla Blanford is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student writer intern with the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: To take or not to take: that is the PSAT and preACT question

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team claimed a big 3-0 sweep of Castro Valley on Thursday, October 1 at Binks Rawlings Gym, improving their record to 14-8 with five matches left in the regular season. The victory marked the school’s first win over the Trojans since 2018, a testament to the program’s progress over the last two years. “Castro Valley may have been undermanned, but we didn’t blink or let off. We had strong play in all three sets, and that’s what we want. The girls stayed really focused,” co-head coach Mike Glass said. This year’s volleyball team is already among the school’s best in the last decade based its record. Their 14 wins is the most since 2017 when the team went 16-8. Other top teams in school history include 2013 when they went 19-11, the 2012 team (18- 15), 2009 (22-9), and 2008’s alltime best team that went 24-6 and reached the D4 North Coast Section Championship. Piedmont hasn’t won an NCS game since 2015, making that the goal of this year’s team. “We’re making steady progress. There’s a lot we still want to work on, so we just want to keep doing our best to improve. I think we’re playing our best right now. We have moments where we lock in against our top competition, so we want to see that all the time,” Glass said. “Year after year, the Piedmont program is strengthening more and more. In this game, we came out with a bunch of energy every single set. We just played our own game,” junior middle hitter Lucia Dorsey mentioned. Against Castro Valley, PHS was without starting outside hitters Fiona Olsen and Sofia Meyer. It led to big games by Dorsey with 10 kills, Nora Trombi with seven kills, and Olivia Stevens with five. Glass called Dorsey’s performance her best of the season. “Where a lot of the power came from was from Corina [Vora’s] sets. She encouraged some of our plays between me Staff Photos Lucia Dorsey had 10 kills in Piedmont’s win vs. Castro Valley. Nora Trombi had seven kills against the Trojans. Olivia Stevens had five kills against Castro Valley. and Maika [Ting]. My chemistry with the setters is becoming super strong,” Dorsey said. Match Recap Piedmont won by scores of 25-21, 25-17, 25-17 over the visiting Trojans. In the first set, Piedmont trailed 4-2 before scoring four straight points to take a 6-4 advantage and never relinquished the lead. Both teams traded points with PHS holding an 18-14 lead, then scored on three straight kills by Izara Dando, and two by Trombi. Castro Valley closed the gap to 23-20, but Piedmont scored two of the final three points with kills by Trombi and Dorsey. PHS opened to a 5-1 lead in the second set, but CV battled back to take a 6-5 lead. The Highlanders regained the lead at 7-6 and maintained their advantage from then on. After that, Piedmont scored seven of nine points to take a commanding 14-9 lead and extended to 21-13. They finished with four of the closing eight points to win 25-17. Castro Valley started with a 4-2 lead in the third set, but Piedmont took control with a run nine straight points with two kills by Maika Ting. CV inched closer to 12-7 but PHS scored three straight with kills by Ting and a block by Dorsey Final stats: Ting had 13 kills and 11 digs. Charlotte Bailey had three kills, two blocks and one dig. Dando had three kills and seven digs. Trombi had seven kills and two digs. Stevens had five kills, two aces, and 14 digs. Dorsey had 10 kills, one ace, and one block.. Allyson Huynh had 16 digs and four assists. Corina Vora had two aces, nine digs and 25 assists. Hazel Schaeffer had 11 digs. Mia Bechtel had one ace, four digs and seven assists. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont dominated American 53-6, improving their league record to 6-4 and y close to clinching a North Coast Section berth. Pictured are Naiya Alexander (left), Edie Elmquist, and Skye Prata Baack. It was a big night for the flag football team when hosting American on Thursday, October 1, The Highlanders beat the visiting Eagles by a one-sided 53-6 score. The result improves Piedmont’s record to 7-8 overall and 6-4 against Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division competition. With four games left in the regular season, Piedmont needs one win to assure a .500 league record going into the WACC tournament on October 20. “To be honest, I have not even spoke about NCS yet to the team. We’ve talked about our record in league and what we want to accomplish in the league, so our focus has been that. What I did talk to them about tonight is getting to the line, being intense, getting out quickly, and being prepared at the line. That intensity takes us into the rest of the season,” coach Beth Black said. One player who has emerged as a defensive leader is Nea Mafi as the team’s new starting safety. She’s filling big shoes left by Class of 2026 starter Dahlia Osman, who finished her high school career with 24 interceptions. Mafi is often acting as the defense’s signal caller, communicating with her other defensive teammates before the snap. She had an interception returned for a touchdown against American. “She is a leader when she’s on the field and on the sideline. She’s constantly watching the game, and that’s helping her improve,” Black said of Mafi. “I’m the safety and the last line of defense. It’s important to keep up communication because I see what the game from a different angle at safety. In the beginning of the season, I wasn’t as communicative. I didn’t know exactly how to get my voice out, but I’ve gotten more and more comfortable with the team, so I slowly started to learn it’s okay to be loud,” Mafi said. Game Recap After American punted on its opening possession, Piedmont scored on its very first offensive play on a short pass to Naiya Alexander that turned into a 50-yard catch and run. The receiver weaved her way around three defenders to doge tackles on the play, sprinting to the end zone. PHS converted a one-point try on a pass from Edie Elmquist to Sydney Latvala to give them a 7-0 lead with 4:52 left in the first quarter. With American pushed back to their own five, Piedmont’s next score was an interception returned for a touchdown by Nea Mafi with 2:59 left. Elmquist completed a pass to Alexander for the onepoint conversion, making it 14-0. PHS scored again with 1:22 left in the first. This time, Elquist found Latvala on a 15-yard pass, making it 20-0 after a missed extra point. American answered with its only touchdown with 7:01 remaining in the second quarter. The Highlanders scored on its ensuing possession on a 10-play, 66-yard drive. They converted a 4th-and-3 in the process at the Eagles’ 23 with an eight-yard run by Mafi and capped off with a nine-yard quarterback keeper by Elmquist. They converted another one-point try on a pass to Latvala, now 27-6 with 2:30 left. They scored again with 8:36 left in the third quarter on a sixplay, 66-yard series. This time, Skye Prata Baack made a nice catch on a near 10-yard pass by Elmquist for the score, making it 33-6 after a missed conversion. Piedmont’s final three touchdowns were not recorded due to an overlap in sports schedules. Details were not provided, but two scores were logged by Zoya Shulze and one by Latvala. With American pushed back to their own five, Piedmont’s next score was an interception returned for a touchdown by Nea Mafi with 2:59 left. Elmquist completed a pass to Alexander for the onepoint conversion, making it 14-0. PHS scored again with 1:22 left in the first. This time, Elquist found Latvala on a 15-yard pass, making it 20-0 after a missed extra point. American answered with its only touchdown with 7:01 remaining in the second quarter. The Highlanders scored on its ensuing possession on a 10-play, 66-yard drive. They converted a 4th-and-3 in the process at the Eagles’ 23 with an eight-yard run by Mafi and capped off with a nine-yard quarterback keeper by Elmquist. They converted another one-point try on a pass to Latvala, now 27-6 with 2:30 left. They scored again with 8:36 left in the third quarter on a sixplay, 66-yard series. This time, Skye Prata Baack made a nice catch on a near 10-yard pass by Elmquist for the score, making it 33-6 after a missed conversion. Piedmont’s final three touchdowns were not recorded due to an overlap in sports schedules. Details were not provided, but two scores were logged by Zoya Shulze and one by Latvala. articles.text: Festival Opera’s Salon Series continues October 25 with Mad Scenes, a concert featuring sopranos Aura Veruni and Lila Khazoum and pianist Daniel Lockert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The 4 p.m. performance will feature scenes from operas including Mozart’s Idomeneo and The Magic Flute, Verdi’s Macbeth, Donizetti’s Anna Bolena and Lucia di Lammermoor, and Ambroise Thomas’ Hamlet. The program will explore the darker and more theatrical side of opera, with costumes by designer Marina Polakoff and props incorporated into the performance to help tell the stories. The concert is scheduled just before Halloween and will highlight the macabre and unhinged elements of opera. Audience members are invited to attend in costume. Veruni and Khazoum are both acclaimed sopranos who will perform the featured scenes with Lockert accompanying on piano. The concert is part of Festival Opera’s three-concert Salon Series, which is presented at the Lila Khazoum Piedmont Center for the Arts. The series concludes November 22 with baritone Efraín Solís, making his Festival Opera debut, accompanied by San Francisco Opera pianist Marika Yasuda. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is at 801 Magnolia Ave. in Piedmont. Tickets for the October 25 concert are $40. Visit festivalopera.org/salon-series to purchase tickets.

articles.text: This year’s festival will feature more than 50 illuminated art displays. Autumn Lights Festival, an art-filled and family-friendly fundraising event for the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt (FGLM), returns this year on Thursday, October 15. Now in its 15th year, the threenight festival brings illuminated art installations to the gardens surrounding Lake Merritt. The event has drawn more than 12,000 visitors since its launch in 2012. This year’s festival will feature more than 50 illuminated art displays throughout the gardens, along with live entertainment, an art market, children’s activities and food and beverage vendors. Additional activities include a costume contest for children and adults, an artist awards program and a kids zone. The festival’s food court will feature local food trucks and vendors, along with beer and wine gardens. Proceeds from ticket sales benefit the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt, a nonprofit volunteer organization formed in 2004. The organization works with the City of Oakland to support the maintenance, revitalizaPhoto by John Kirkmire tion and programming of the gardens at Lakeside Park. The seven-acre collection of themed gardens includes the Bonsai Garden, Sensory Garden, Toddler Garden and Urban Edible Garden, among others. FGLM volunteers provide maintenance assistance as the city’s gardening staff has been reduced over time. The Autumn Lights Festival is the organization’s largest annual fundraiser. Tickets and additional information are available through the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt at https://gardensatlakemerritt.org/about/.

articles.text: Filoli’s “Nightfall Halloween” event is underway at the historic Woodside estate, with more than 53,000 tickets sold across its fall programs following a sold-out opening weekend. “Nightfall” runs now through November 1 and is open from 5:30 to 10 p.m. The Halloween event features more than 1,000 illuminated jack-o’-lanterns, more than 200 scarecrows, character actors, food trucks and Halloween-themed attractions throughout Filoli’s historic house and gardens. New this year is a Witches’ Village in the redwoods, featuring a 20-foot witches’ cauldron, woven wicker witches, live banjo music and haunted railway conductors. The new Haunted Railway includes more than 1,000 feet of track through the redwoods, with miniature houses and other handcrafted elements along the route. Nightfall is in its third year as a large-scale Halloween event at Filoli. The event had sold more than 32,000 tickets before the end of summer, according to Filoli. A Nightfall Champagne Lounge is also offered at 5:30, 7 and 8:30 p.m. The 60-minute experience in Filoli’s Historic Ballroom includes three pours from a champagne flight and admission to Nightfall. Filoli said the Champagne Lounge also provides admission on some nights when general admission tickets have sold out. During the day, Filoli is hosting Autumn Days through November 1 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. The daytime program includes a pumpkin patch, fall decorations, harvest games, seasonal food and drinks, and photo opportunities. Tickets and information are available at www.filoli.org. The Halloween event features more than 1,000 illuminated jack-o’-lanterns. Photo courtesy of Filoli

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is presenting Peter Pan Goes Wrong, a comedy about an amateur theater company attempting to stage Peter Pan while a series of mishaps threatens to derail the production. Written by Henry Lewis, Henry Shields and Jonathan Sayer, the play follows the fictional Cornley Polytechnic Drama Society as its members take on J.M. Barrie’s classic story. The production features flying rigs, sword fights and a crocodile, along with forgotten lines, malfunctioning scenery and rivalries that spill onto the stage. The play is by the creators of The Play That Goes Wrong, which similarly follows a fictional theater troupe whose production goes increasingly awry. Peter Pan Goes Wrong premiered in London in 2013 before later moving to the West End and Broadway. Susi Damilano directs the San Francisco production. The cast includes Greg Ayers, Joe Ayers, Maggie Mason, Christian McCooey, Ezra Reaves, Renee Rogoff, Patrick Russell, Sophie Schulman, Terrance Austin Smith, Jomar Tagatac and Phaedra Tillery-Boughton, among others. The production runs through November 28 at San Francisco Playhouse, 450 Post St. in San Francisco’s Union Square neighborhood. Performances are Tuesday through Sunday, with evening and matinee performances on select days. The show runs approximately two hours and five minutes, including a 15-minute intermission, and is recommended for ages 8 and older. Tickets and information for Peter Pan Goes Wrong and additional shows and musicals are available at sfplayhouse.org/. Scene from Peter Pan Goes Wrong. Photo by Jeremy Daniel

articles.text: Sale held Oct. 17–18 San Francisco Opera hosts a costume collection sale in Burlingame October 17 and 18, offering shoppers the chance to purchase theatrical garments and accessories from decades of productions at the War Memorial Opera House. The two-day sale will take place at the company’s Scene Shop in Burlingame, with items ranging from Victorian dresses and Edwardian ensembles to 1920s fashions, military uniforms, capes and fantasy costumes. The collection includes pieces from productions such as Luisa Miller, Un Ballo in Maschera, Idomeneo, Fidelio and Don Giovanni. Prices will range from $5 to $525, with premium items priced higher. Stage props and other opera merchandise will also be available. The sale offers opportunities for collectors, performers and others seeking distinctive clothing for Halloween, Renaissance fairs, theatrical productions and masquerades. San Francisco Opera periodically holds costume sales to make room for new productions. Proceeds from admission fees and sales will support the company. The public sale will run from 9:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. both days, with the last entry at 4:30 p.m. Timed-entry tickets are required and include two hours of shopping. Admission ranges from $5 to $25, depending on the day and time. Prices will range from $5 to $525. Photo courtesy of San Francisco Opera

articles.text: Escher String Quartet Music at Kohl Mansion will open its 44th season on October 18, with a performance by the Escher String Quartet, an internationally recognized chamber ensemble based in New York City. The Escher String Quartet features Adam Barnett-Hart and Bryan Lee on violin, Pierre Lapointe on viola and Brook Speltz on cello. Formed in 2005 and named for Dutch graphic artist M.C. Escher, the quartet is known for performances combining technical precision, interpretive depth and a distinctive ensemble sound. The program will feature three works from the string quartet repertoire: Haydn’s Quartet in G major, Op. 76, No. 1; Shostakovich’s Quartet No. 3 in F major, Op. 73; and Brahms’ Quartet in A minor, Op. 51, No. 2. The Escher String Quartet serves as Artists of the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center and has performed at venues and festivals including Wigmore Hall in London, the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam, the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., and the Auditorium du Louvre in Paris. The ensemble has received several honors, including an Avery Fisher Career Grant and Lincoln Center’s Martin E. Segal Award. Its recording projects have included the complete string quartets of composers Alexander Zemlinsky and Felix Mendelssohn. The concert will begin at 7 p.m. at Kohl Mansion, 2750 Adeline Drive in Burlingame. A pre-concert talk by Stanford cellist and educator Christopher Costanza will begin at 6 p.m., followed by a complimentary glass of wine and dessert after the performance at 9 p.m. Music at Kohl Mansion’s 2026- 27 season includes eight performances through May 2, 2027, featuring chamber music ensembles and artists from the United States and Europe. Performances take place in the historic Kohl Mansion, also known as The Oaks, which was built in 1914 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982. Tickets and season subscriptions are available at www.musicatkohl.org.
articles.title: Music at Kohl Mansion opens 44th season with Escher String Quartet

articles.text: What does it mean to find your voice—and a place to belong? The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) will explore that question at its 2026 Benefit Concert & Auction, “The Sound of Home,” at 6 p.m. on Saturday, October 10, at the DoubleTree by Hilton Berkeley Marina. The evening will celebrate extraordinary young singers and the community of families, educators, alumni, volunteers, accompanists, and supporters who make their musical journey possible. Led by award-winning Artistic Director Eric Tuan, the evening will feature performances by PEBCC singers, including the Ensemble Choir, along with two special guest soloists: alumna Kate Offer, a classical singer and conductor, and PEBCC singer Naomi Walker, who recently received the 1st Prize Solo Competition award at the Golden Gate International Choral Festival. For Tuan, a world-class choral education is about far more than learning to sing. “Choral music is one of the most powerful ways for young people to build connections with each other and the world around them,” says Tuan. “Our singers learn to listen to each other, to share their voices in a way that empowers the whole team, and to explore different cultures and perspectives through the universal language of music. As our alumni remind us, those experiences last for a lifetime.” At the heart of PEBCC’s mission is the belief that every young person should have the opportunity to experience that journey, regardless of financial circumstances. Financial assistance is central to the organization’s commitment to building a community where every singer belongs. The benefit concert supports that mission while celebrating the full circle of community surrounding the choir. “Our singers are part of a community much bigger than themselves,” says Tuan. “The transformative experiences singers experience wouldn’t be possible without the alumni who come back to teach and volunteer, the families who support them through the program, and the supporters who give so generously of their time, talent, and treasure to ensure every singer finds a home at PEBCC.” Tickets are available at piedmontchoirs.org. PEBCC’s Online Silent Auction opened Saturday, October 3, at 9:00 a.m. and closes Sunday, October 11, at 11:00 p.m. The 2026 Benefit Concert & Auction is made possible through the generous support of Bell Investment Advisors, Commercial Bank of California, and Anonymous Foundation. Sponsorship helps PEBCC provide transformative musical experiences and keep many choir and festival events free and accessible, enriching the cultural life of the Bay Area. To learn about becoming a Benefit Sponsor, contact Natalie Titone at ntitone@ piedmontchoirs.org.

The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), California’s oldest youth orchestra and the second-oldest in the United States, announces its landmark 90th Anniversary Season, celebrating nine decades of guiding young musicians toward excellence through orchestral music, education, and community. The 2026–27 anniversary season will feature four concerts spanning music from across centuries and cultures. Founded in Berkeley in 1936 by conductor Jessica Marcelli, when women conductors were exceedingly rare, YPSO enters its 90th season following a successful concert tour of Finland and Sweden in June 2026. From its Berkeley roots, the orchestra has grown to bring together young musicians from across the San Francisco Bay Area. Today, under Music Director and Conductor David Ramadanoff, YPSO continues a tradition of challenging young musicians with great orchestral repertoire while fostering accomplishment, community, and a lifelong passion for music. “I’m very proud to be part of an organization that has been providing young people the opportunity to play great music for 90 seasons,” Ramadanoff said. “During my 38 years as Music Director, it has been exciting and heartwarming to help this orchestra develop into an outstanding ensemble capable of playing the wonderful and challenging music we have programmed this season.” The season starts with the fall concert on Saturday, November 7, 2026, at 7:30 p.m., at First Church Berkeley. YPSO will open its 90th season with Shostakovich’s Festival Overture, Debussy’s Nocturnes, and Brahms’ Symphony No. 1. The winter concert will take place on Saturday, February 20, 2027, at 7:30 p.m., at First Church Berkeley. The winter concert features Tchaikovsky’s Romeo and Juliet Fantasy-Overture, Gabriela Lena Frank’s Three Latin American Dances, and other works, including music by Ralph Vaughan Williams. The spring concert is on Saturday, May 1, 2027, at 7:30 p.m., at First Church Berkeley. They’ll play Verdi’s Overture to La forza del destino, Dvořák’s Symphony No. 6, and additional repertoire. The season culminates on Sunday, June 6, 2027, at 3 p.m. (venue TBA) with a special 90th Anniversary Pops Concert, bringing together current YPSO musicians with alumni from across generations of the orchestra’s history. Former YPSO musicians will be invited to return, reconnect, and play alongside the next generation, celebrating the lasting community YPSO has built over nine decades. The program is expected to feature Arturo Márquez’s Danzón No. 2 and a festive selection of audience favorites from stage and screen, creating a joyful celebration of YPSO’s past, present, and future. The 2026–27 season honors YPSO’s 90-year legacy by bringing together generations of musicians through the music and community that continue to connect them. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, October 7, 2026 PEBCC celebrates “The Sound of Home” at 2026 benefit concert & auction What does it mean to find your voice—and a place to belong? The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) will explore that question at its 2026 Benefit Concert & Auction, “The Sound of Home,” at 6 p.m. on Saturday, October 10, at the DoubleTree by Hilton Berkeley Marina. The evening will celebrate extraordinary young singers and the community of families, educators, alumni, volunteers, accompanists, and supporters who make their musical journey possible. Led by award-winning Artistic Director Eric Tuan, the evening will feature performances by PEBCC singers, including the Ensemble Choir, along with two special guest soloists: alumna Kate Offer, a classical singer and conductor, and PEBCC singer Naomi Walker, who recently received the 1st Prize Solo Competition award at the Golden Gate International Choral Festival. For Tuan, a world-class choral education is about far more than learning to sing. “Choral music is one of the most powerful ways for young people to build connections with each other and the world around them,” says Tuan. “Our singers learn to listen to each other, to share their voices in a way that empowers the whole team, and to explore different cultures and perspectives through the universal language of music. As our alumni remind us, those experiences last for a lifetime.” At the heart of PEBCC’s mission is the belief that every young person should have the opportunity to experience that journey, regardless of financial circumstances. Financial assistance is central to the organization’s commitment to building a community where every singer belongs. The benefit concert supports that mission while celebrating the full circle of community surrounding the choir. “Our singers are part of a community much bigger than themselves,” says Tuan. “The transformative experiences singers experience wouldn’t be possible without the alumni who come back to teach and volunteer, the families who support them through the program, and the supporters who give so generously of their time, talent, and treasure to ensure every singer finds a home at PEBCC.” Tickets are available at piedmontchoirs.org. articles.text: Braving another warm day on Sept. 30, the last day of the month, 50 members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group and five of their canine companions gathered at the Exedra excited to see if Nace Avenue really is nice. Leading our walk and tour was Pat Keller, a long-time Piedmont resident and Wednesday walker. Having lived on Nace Avenue for years, Pat was well qualified to relate the history of the area and provide information about some of the homes. We began the walk heading in the direction of Dracena Park. As we walked through the park on our way to Nace, Park Commissioner Jack Fischrup noted that there are now four great horned owls in residence. Nace is a tiny street with 27 houses. One unusual feature of Nace is that it’s L-shaped, making a 90-degree turn toward the middle. The street was named after Frank C. Havens’ secretary, John Nace. At the time, it was common to name streets after the people who were involved in developing the city. Nace is now a popular street for young families, with approximately 28 kids on it. The first house we visited was 22 Nace. It was built in 1906 for $2,820. We were fortunate enough to encounter one of the owners, KT, who graciously invited us to come into her magnificent backyard. It’s a breathtaking and fun little surprise when you enter the rear. The first thing you notice is the immensity of the outdoor living space with beautiful views of Piedmont. In addition there was a hot tub surrounded by redwood decking, a wooden, round-shaped sauna with a cold plunge adjacent, and an outdoor shower. To top things off, an inviting outdoor cabana with sofas tempted some of the walkers to sit and relax. Leaving 22 Nace, we walked down the street to 42 Nace, which has an uncommon flat roof. Pat explained to the group that a fire in the 1950s destroyed the original pitched roof which was then replaced by the flat roof. Continuing just next door, we visited 46 Nace, the present residence of Dave and Kathy Yam. Known as the “Gibson house,” it was built in 1910 by the Fenton family of ice cream fame. The original house had lath and plaster walls and the beams were first generation old-growth redwood. The Smith family moved in around 1912 and the home remained in the family until 1991 (79 years!). It is reported that they planted the large Catalpa tree out front, which is now a Piedmont Heritage Tree. However, a neighbor, Mrs. Gibson, claimed to have grown up at 46 Nace and her father planted the tree. Winnifred inherited the house and married Orrin Smith sometime between 1940 and 1950. They had no children, but all of the family celebrations were held at the house. Orrin was a wood shop teacher at McClymonds High School in Oakland and had a great workshop in the basement. The shelves and drawers for storing hardware were built by his students as a shop project. Orrin and Winnifred remodeled the house extensively both inside and outside, excavating a basement and using the surplus soil to level the backyard. Next, they dug out the front and built a garage. In 1976, Winnifred started the “Nace is Nice” block party to celebrate the Fourth of July. The current owner, Kathy, inherited the block party tradition and revived it in the 1990s. When Winnifred passed away, her sister Barbara became the executor of the estate. Barbara was the mother of one of Kathy Yam’s best friends. At the time, Kathy and her husband Dave Among those participating were Denny McGee, Jim Kuo, Deborah Curtin with K-9 best friend Brie, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Jim Kellogg, Liz Dalrymple, Mark Davis, Lisa Euphrat, Stacy Venetluhmamm, Judy Love, Susie Backer, Caskey Weston, Marianne Jakus, Sherry Jacobs, Peggy Shultz, Noemi Alvarado, Quincy Dong, Juliane Jacqueline, Debbie Powell, Judy Wang, Cathy Laymon, Stella Houston, Lois Price, Brenda Ferrero, Matt Gerhardt, Pat Keller, Helen Dong, Claudine Bach, Albert Chen, Irene Thompson, Tom Lehrkind, Mike Gallant, Joan Jung with K-9 best friend JT, Dan Scdonis, Dave DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Ken Hubbert, Joyce Ahern, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, and Nancy DeRoche. The group was pleased to welcome Norman and Carol Quan, Holly Hansen with K-9 best friend Ginger, and Adam Hundt who were walking with them for the first time.

articles.text: High in the French Alps, where vineyards cling to steep slopes beneath snow-capped peaks, the wines of Savoie are gaining attention for their distinctive character and sense of place. For generations, Savoie’s vineyards have been closely tied to the region’s mountain communities. Today, a new generation of winemakers is bringing renewed energy to an area once known primarily to French locals and Alpine holidaymakers. The result is a collection of wines that can be remarkably fresh, mineral-driven and unlike those produced in France’s better-known regions. White wines dominate Savoie’s production, with the Jacquère grape playing a central role. Light-bodied and crisp, Jacquère produces wines with lively acidity and subtle floral and citrus notes, making them natural companions to local mountain cuisine. Altesse, another important white grape, produces the more structured and aromatic wines known as Roussette de Savoie. My favorite wine is Chignin-Bergeron, which is made from the Rhone Valley’s Roussanne grape. The region also has its own red specialties. Mondeuse, a traditional local grape, creates deeply colored wines with bright acidity, peppery spice and dark-fruit flavors. Gamay and Pinot Noir are also planted, adding further variety to the region’s offerings. Savoie’s geography is central to its identity. Vineyards are scattered across valleys and foothills, often at considerable elevations. The cool Alpine climate allows grapes to ripen slowly while retaining the acidity that gives the wines their characteristic freshness. That freshness is particularly well suited to Savoie’s traditional foods: fondue, raclette, tartiflette and other rich mountain dishes. The wines cut through the richness of the cheese and potatoes, creating a pairing that reflects the region itself. As interest in distinctive, terroir-driven wines continues to grow, Savoie is increasingly finding a place on the international wine map. Its bottles offer something increasingly sought after by modern wine drinkers: wines with a strong sense of origin, tradition and landscape. articles.text: At the foot of Mont Granier in France’s Alpine Savoie region, the name Philippe Viallet has become closely associated with the area’s distinctive wines. The family wine story began in 1966, when Marcel and Yvonne Viallet acquired a small vineyard in Apremont. Their sons, Pierre and Philippe, later continued the family business, with Philippe helping to develop it into both a wine producer and wine merchant. The Viallet range reflects the diversity of Savoie’s mountain vineyards. Among its bestknown wines is Apremont, made from the Jacquère grape. It is a light, crisp and refreshing white wine with bright acidity. Another important wine is Chignin-Bergeron, made from the Roussanne grape and generally fuller and more aromatic, with flavors of ripe fruit and flowers. Roussette de Savoie, made from the Altesse grape, offers another distinctive style, while the winery’s red wines include Mondeuse, one of Savoie’s traditional varieties, as well as Pinot Noir and Gamay. The winery also produces Crémant de Savoie, a sparkling wine, along with rosé wines. Philippe Viallet’s wines offer a taste of the Alpine landscape. Fresh, lively and closely connected to local grape varieties, they demonstrate why Savoie is attracting growing interest from wine drinkers looking for wines with a strong sense of place and a character of their own.

By Sierra Berrick The world of competitive dog sports can be one of the most exciting for canine enthusiasts. There is the opportunity to meet fellow dog lovers, win awards for your pup, and spend quality time with them. Unfortunately, fewer and fewer new people are joining. Let’s examine a couple of reasons that may explain this, and hopefully drive current professionals in the American Kennel Club (AKC) world to make some changes. Not everything is the fault of individuals, but of our infrastructure. Simply put, money is an issue. With the costs of operating training clubs and events going up just like the cost of living, many people are being priced out of dog shows. To enter a dog in AKC conformation, the majority of shows cost around $37 a day. To compete in a four-day show, that’s well over $100, not counting the cost of travel and food. Even newer sports, such as Fast CAT, demonstrate significant costs on their entry forms. In California, pre-entry for Fast CAT, which allows two runs per dog per day, costs between $28 and $35 per run. Considering this sport is entirely based on participation, the unfortunate truth is that people are now paying for their titles rather than needing to demonstrate excellence with their dog. For young people who may have bachelor’s-degree-level jobs, these prohibitively high entry fees make it impossible for them to get their foot in the door. Lack of new exhibitors is a big concern, not just because it means dog shows are slowly becoming an event only for the wealthy, but because fewer competitors means fewer championship points and majors. The AKC point system is based on winning against a certain number of dogs, and with more competitors aging out than entering the sport, it will become markedly harder for individuals to achieve championship titles with their dogs. Now let’s talk about attitude. Many people coming from pet backgrounds assume that all dog people are enthusiastic and kind. Unfortunately, this is not always so within the dog show world. Many new participants at dog shows report feeling unwelcome and unsupported. Although there is no clear reason for this, the idea of people simply being competitive does not fully explain it. The high costs of entry, plus feeling excluded by veterans in the sport, unfortunately lead many new exhibitors to quit before they’ve really started. This means that it is up to the old-timers in dog sports to open their hearts to new competitors, and for new competitors to set the tone in the sport as welcoming going forward. Perhaps the American Kennel Club should consider the long-term results of pricing out exhibitors with these high entry fees. Only time will tell if dog enthusiasts are able to commit to these necessary changes. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. articles.text: Part 2 in a series It all started with the water. It smelled awful, but it made his old joints feel better. In the mid- 1850s, old Isaac Holmes dragged a bathtub down the ravine to the mineral springs on the side of the hill. Soaking in the mineral water helped to ease his rheumatism. When he died, the mineral springs were forgotten. In the 1860s, these mineral springs (said to contain sulphur, magnesia, iodine and iron) were re-discovered in the ravine behind today’s Exedra, the current location of Bushy Dell Creek. Drinking or soaking in mineral water was believed to have great curative powers. These mineral springs were similar to the popular mineral waters in Calistoga, and they were only three miles from downtown Oakland. Investors quickly saw an opportunity to develop the springs and build a hotel to accommodate visitors who came to “take the waters.” They selected the name “Piedmont,” meaning “foot of the hills,” thus securing the name of Piedmont to our locale. The investors formed the Piedmont Land Company to buy 350 acres around the ravine, build the hotel and sell any adjoining land not needed for the hotel purposes as residential lots. In 1871, the Piedmont Springs Hotel opened near today’s Exedra as a first-class resort. The photo of the hotel shows only the northern portion of the building, which had two wings and was twice the size of the building as shown. The hotel had a wide veranda, 20 first-class bedrooms and two suites, five dining rooms, telegraph service, and a Grand Saloon (for men only) with an elegant mahogany bar, billiard table, spittoons and a pot-bellied stove. The ladies’ entrance allowed women to enter the hotel, avoid the saloon and proceed directly to the main dining room with its crystal chandelier, linen tablecloths and fine china. The hotel quickly became a popular destination and drew visitors who passed a pleasant Sunday at Piedmont Springs, strolling the meandering paths to the mineral springs and enjoying an excellent lunch or dinner. articles.text: Happy Fall, all! THE VALUE OF LOCAL REPRESENTATION: An exceptionally strong class of motivated buyers is fueling heavy demand in Piedmont right now, proving that the fall market remains a fantastic opportunity to sell before the season winds down for winter. This localized window offers sellers a great time to achieve excellent results with careful preparation and local expertise. For buyers, navigating our fast-moving, highly competitive market is always easier with local representation by your side. Working with a local agent brings a few distinct advantages: • Exclusive Insight: Local agents are often the first to know about unique opportunities around town, including quiet, off-market properties. • Intimate Inventory Knowledge: They tour the inventory firsthand and know recent neighborhood sales that make good comparables, often with in-depth knowledge of properties and their condition to help put a new listing’s true value into perspective. • Good Neighbors: Over the years, local agents build real friendships and trust with colleagues across different brokerages. When things get competitive, that mutual respect and track record of smooth closings can be the comfort a listing agent needs to help choose your offer. MORTGAGE MONEY Our “go-to” Mortgage Money Broker, BRADY THOMAS, LA SALLE MORTGAGE, has this to share this month: Mortgage rates have moved sharply higher over the past month, and last week the Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time in more than three years. With inflation heating back up, energy costs rising and the war with Iran continuing, homeowners should be prepared for mortgage rates to stay higher for longer. From my seat as a mortgage lender, higher rates are becoming just as much a seller problem as a buyer problem. I’m talking with more buyers who recognize that when a home needs work, has been sitting, or is priced too aggressively, they have leverage. Instead of simply asking for a lower price, buyers are more frequently negotiating seller credits that can be used to lower their mortgage rate or cover closing costs. This is often the most effective way to bridge the affordability gap. Sellers with the best homes may not need to make these concessions, but everyone else should understand that buyers will increasingly look to sellers for help with the economic pain in the mortgage markets.

articles.text: Nancy Beninati (NancyforPiedmont.com) I support and appreciate the hard work of our police, fire, and city employees. I believe all Piedmont employees should be paid fairly and competitively, consistent with what the City can responsibly afford. The City must carefully evaluate any proposals and the longterm fiscal impacts to make a decision that best serves our community as a whole. While Piedmont has some wealthy residents, the City’s revenue streams are limited and rely heavily on property taxes. Any significant increase in compensation or benefits must be considered in the context of the entire City budget, the needs of all City employees, and other important City priorities. I support Measure GG because it would provide the City with additional ongoing revenue for parks, recreation, infrastructure, maintenance, and other City needs, including employee compensation. But additional revenue does not eliminate the need to make difficult budget choices. As a councilmember, I would support fair compensation while also making sure that any agreement is financially sustainable and treats all of our employees fairly. Ultimately, the Council and City will have to balance competitive compensation with the City’s overall financial constraints and the priorities of the community. Adam Hundt (AdamHundt.com) The City Council should present to the community a comprehensive plan for the police and fire departments. We need to maintain these services for the future in a way that is fair to the union members and ensures that the departments are adequately funded. Currently, overtime salaries are 136% of the amount approved for the budget year (a cost increase of $927,150). This is not sustainable for overtime firefighters or for the city. Is the solution increasing the number of staff, changing the shift schedule, altering the duties (in addition to extinguishing fires, Piedmont firefighters are also trained as EMTs or paramedics), or something else? I believe everyone in the community deserves adequate health care. The plan the Council should produce must assure health benefits for the union and every other city employee. Finally, we should explore ways to provide housing for Piedmont city employees. One way to do this is to work with developers to build below-market-rate units specifically for municipal employees such as firefighters, police, and teachers. I’m eager to work on this plan, and I promise to submit it to the whole community for comment. Sunny Bostrom-Fleming One of the main benefits of living in Piedmont is public safety. Protecting the lives of our families and our pets is our number one priority; our property can be replaced, but the lives we cherish cannot. While we are all very proud of both our police and fire departments, we must maintain a competitive workplace for these fine people. Our current focus is the fire department. Where do we get the operator funds to make sure we are a very competitive community? Every day when they leave their homes they have no guarantee of returning alive or uninjured. Measure GG, which is vital to keeping our community financially sound, could go a long way toward funding the fire department. I want us to consider additional funding, such as the schools have with the Giving Campaign. Seeing how we are surrounded by one of the most dangerous cities in America, Oakland reported 35,096 crimes in 2024: 6,000-plus auto burglaries, 1,100 residential burglaries, and 86 murders. Piedmont had 76 burglaries, one assault, and over 70 stolen cars. Our police and fire professionals are our first line of defense. The officers of Rome who led from the front lines earned their rank through merit and bravery. Tom Ramsey Incumbent (vote4tomramsey.com) Piedmont’s first responders are hometown heroes. While many families move here for the schools, we all value our top-quality police and firefighters who keep us safe every day. As a small town, Piedmont is in a tough spot to match compensation packages offered by larger cities or towns that benefit from bigger budgets and commercial tax revenue. For decades, Piedmont navigated this position by determining salary levels through an independent third-party that conducts a salary survey comparing total compensation for each role against 13 Bay Area cities identified as comparable to Piedmont. Pay rates for each role are set based on the median compensation. Recruitment challenges are regional, and responsible budgeting requires balancing new requests such as increased healthcare benefits with existing city obligations, where retiree and current employee medical premiums already cost the city $4 million annually. I acknowledge this process is taking too long, and it weighs heavily on all involved. I am committed to continuing transparent, good-faith dialogue through our established bargaining representatives to reach a sustainable agreement that is both fair to all employees and fiscally responsible to the community.

articles.text: Honorable Mentions Maddy Huynh earns an honorable mention for making a huge impact on the girls’ tennis varsity roster as a freshman, typically appearing at No. 3 singles, which a few appearances in the No. 2 spot. In September, the freshman won eight matches and lost just twice – both of which went to an extra third set. Dylan Jerez earns an honorable mention for his instant impact on the boys’ water polo team as their starting goalie as a sophomore. He had 12 saves, a steal, and assist in Piedmont’s 14-6 win over Encinal, 10 saves and five assists in a 15-11 win over Bishop O’Dowd on September 4, and nine saves in their 8-7 double overtime loss to James Logan on September 3. Sophomore Dylan Jerez earns an honorable mention for his impact as the new water polo goalie.
